arc_intro:
FQ-218 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

Two things this lesson. First — Meera just called. She has a board meeting tomorrow and one of the questions will be 'which team owns which cost line item in our AWS bill.' I told her I'd have an answer. I need your help getting there.

Second — I want to look at the whole picture before we close this ticket. You've touched every part of this infrastructure. I want to see it drawn out properly, as one coherent architecture, not as individual fixes across six tickets.

— Ravi
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

That's what the architecture looks like now — and that's what we couldn't have drawn 8 months ago at FQ-142 without embarrassing ourselves. Not because we didn't have the resources, but because we didn't understand them.

Meera has her cost breakdown by team. Tagging policy is enforced in CloudFormation now, not just hoped for in a wiki. And I can see the whole thing in one diagram without having to explain 'there's also this thing in us-east-1 that we forgot to mention.'

One last thing before we close FQ-218: I want to formally close FQ-142. The ticket that started all of this. That's the next conversation.

— Ravi

tasks.scenario: Meera needs a cost breakdown by team for her board meeting tomorrow. You open AWS Cost Explorer and try to filter by team — there's no usable dimension to filter on. All resources show up under the same flat account view.
tasks.question: What's the root cause of not being able to break down costs by team, and what would have needed to happen for this to be possible?
options: A) AWS doesn't support per-team cost breakdown — this capability simply doesn't exist

B) Resources need consistent, activated cost allocation TAGS (key-value metadata on each resource, such as Team: order-service, Team: analytics) before Cost Explorer can filter and group by them. Without a tagging strategy applied consistently from the beginning, there's no dimension to filter on
C) Per-team cost breakdown requires setting up a separate AWS account for each team
D) Cost Explorer only shows per-service breakdowns (EC2, RDS, S3) — team-level attribution is impossible regardless of tags
tasks.explanation: Tags without Cost in Explorer filter to do dimension not — resources just flat account in view kaanudhu. Consistent tagging strategy + Cost allocation tags activated in billing = team-level, service-level, project-level filtering possible. This retrospective-a to add very kastam, prospective-a start do easy.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — consistent tags are the prerequisite for any cost attribution capability.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — AWS per-team attribution support does, but tags consistently apply if done it was only. Tagging strategy without, dimension not.

tasks.question: What is an AWS resource tag, and what does 'activating a tag as a cost allocation tag' specifically do?
options: A) Tags are AWS-managed labels automatically applied to all resources; activation makes them permanently visible

B) A tag is a user-defined key-value pair attached to a resource (e.g. Team: order-engineering, Environment: production). Activating a tag as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console tells AWS to include that tag dimension in Cost Explorer reports and cost allocation reports — without activation, the tag exists on the resource but doesn't appear as a filterable dimension in cost reports
C) Tags are only available for EC2 instances and S3 buckets, not other resource types
D) Activating a cost allocation tag automatically applies that tag to all untagged resources in the account
tasks.explanation: Tag — user-defined key-value pair — in resource exist does. But Cost in Explorer filter-a use must do- — , Billing in console cost allocation tag-a activate must do verum. Activate without doing tag in resource is there but cost in reports kaanaaathu — two separate steps.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — tags exist on resources, but cost allocation activation is a separate step in the Billing console.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — tag in resource irundhaalum, cost in reports kbut Billing in console activate must do. Two separate steps, one alone not enough.

tasks.question: What's the practical difference between having a tagging POLICY (documented rules for how to tag) versus just having a tagging CONVENTION (an informal wiki page saying 'please tag your stuff')?
options: A) There's no practical difference — any written guide on tagging is equally effective

B) A tagging policy is enforced (through AWS Config rules, IAM policies, or CloudFormation required tags) so resources cannot be created without required tags; a tagging convention is just a request that people remember, which they frequently don't. Only a policy creates the structural guarantee that tags are actually applied consistently
C) Policies are more expensive to maintain than conventions because they require AWS Config, which has significant per-rule charges
D) Conventions are preferable because they allow more flexibility and are less likely to break deployments
tasks.explanation: Policy enforce does — resource tags without create do cannot (CloudFormation required tags, AWS Config rule, IAM policy). Convention just 'please remember' — people forget, especially when they're in a hurry. Only structural enforcement gives consistent tagging.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — policy enforces structurally, convention relies on memory. Only enforcement creates consistency.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — convention and policy same effect not. Policy enforce does, convention request does. Real difference in outcomes.

tasks.scenario: You pull the current tagging state across the account.

Result: ₹0 cost attribution to any team or service is possible from current billing data
what_to_find: No resource in the entire account has a consistent Team or Environment tag — the Name tag exists on some but is inconsistently applied and not a cost allocation dimension
Cost allocation tags have never been activated in the Billing console — even if some tags existed, they would not appear in Cost Explorer reports
notification-worker has zero tags of any kind — not even a Name tag — making it the most difficult resource to attribute to any team or purpose from billing data alone
This is the exact scenario Meera is facing: a board meeting question ('which team owns this cost') that engineering genuinely cannot answer from AWS billing data today
tasks.correct_fix: Define a mandatory tagging policy (minimum: Team, Environment, and Owner tags required on all resources) and enforce it in CloudFormation templates going forward. Retrospectively apply tags to all existing resources. Activate Team, Environment, and Owner as cost allocation tags in the Billing console. Set up an AWS Config rule to flag any untagged resource going forward.
tasks.explanation: This exact spec mistake confirmed on the actual account — no tagging strategy, no cost allocation. Meera's question legitimate, engineering answer honest-a 'we can't tell you from billing data today.'

tasks.question: Arrange the correct order to fix the tagging gap properly — for both existing resources and future ones.
items: Define the mandatory tag policy (minimum required keys: Team, Environment, Owner)
Retrospectively apply tags to all existing resources across the account
Activate the new tags as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing console
Add required tag enforcement to all CloudFormation templates going forward
Set up an AWS Config rule to flag any resource missing required tags
Verify Cost Explorer now shows cost attribution by Team and Environment after the next billing cycle
tasks.explanation: Policy define must do first (what tags, what values, before applying), then existing resources retroactively tag must do, then in billing activate must do, then future enforcement in templates + Config in rule add must do, LAST-a next billing in cycle verify must do. Billing cycle's delay is there — activate did udane historical data retroactively appear aagathu.
tasks.ren_correct: Nice sequencing — policy first, retroactive application, billing activation, enforcement for future, then verify after the billing cycle.
tasks.ren_wrong: Order think again — policy define without doing tag apply must not. Billing activation and enforcement also separate necessary steps.

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev says: 'Let's just agree on a tagging convention now and everyone tags their stuff going forward. We don't need a hard enforcement rule — the team knows the policy.'
tasks.question: Why is a convention-only approach insufficient as the structural fix here?
options: A) It's actually fine for a small team — enforcement overhead outweighs the benefits for FoodQuick's current size

B) Convention-only relies on everyone remembering to tag every resource, every time, including during urgent deployments and on-call incidents when it's most likely to be forgotten. The entire history of this ticket shows exactly what 'rely on people remembering' produces: 8-month-old TODO comments, indefinite log retention defaults, 6-week-open security misconfigurations. Structural enforcement (required tags in CloudFormation, AWS Config flagging) is what makes the convention actually work
C) AWS prevents any team with fewer than 50 engineers from using tag enforcement
D) Convention is always better than enforcement because enforcement blocks deployments in emergencies
tasks.explanation: This CS2-CS6's whole pattern's direct application — 'people will remember' — we paatha: Vikram's TODO, Deepak's manual SG change, priya.k's subscription, every 'never expire' default. Structural enforcement real fix, convention is the intent, enforcement is what makes it real.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — this entire ticket's history shows what 'rely on people remembering' produces. Enforcement is the structural fix.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — convention-only insufficient, and the evidence is the entire history of this course. Structural enforcement real guarantee.

tasks.scenario: While retroactively tagging existing resources, you reach reporting-db-01. It runs internal analytics reports for ananya-analyst's team, but it lives on infrastructure provisioned and maintained by the platform engineering team. karthik-dev asks: 'Which team do we tag this as — analytics or platform?'
tasks.question: How should ambiguous ownership be resolved in a tagging policy?
options: A) Skip tagging ambiguous resources entirely until ownership is definitively resolved

B) Use multiple tags to capture different dimensions — Owner: platform-engineering (who provisions/maintains the infrastructure), ServiceFor: analytics (what business function it serves) — so both dimensions are captured without forcing a false either/or. The tagging policy should anticipate shared or cross-functional resources and define how to handle them, rather than leaving ambiguity as an excuse not to tag
C) Assign ownership to whichever team uses the resource most, determined by log analysis
D) Platform engineering should own all infrastructure resources without exception, regardless of business function
tasks.explanation: Ambiguous for ownership two-tag approach — Owner (infrastructure responsibility) and ServiceFor (business function) — render both dimensions without either/or compromise. Policy should anticipate this: shared resources are common, 'skip because ambiguous' is the real mistake.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — two dimensions, two tags. Policy should anticipate shared resources, not treat ambiguity as an excuse.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — ambiguous-a even if skip doingle tax loss-a is there. Two separate tag keys solve the either/or problem cleanly.

tasks.scenario: Tags are applied across all existing resources. You open Cost Explorer to show Meera the team-level breakdown — but the Team tag dimension still doesn't appear as a filtering option.
tasks.error_shown:
AWS Cost Explorer — Group By:
Available dimensions: Service, Linked Account, Region, Usage Type, API Operation

(Team, Environment, and Owner tags do not appear as filterable dimensions despite being applied to all resources)
tasks.diagnosis: Resource tags exist on the resources — that part was done correctly. But the separate step of activating them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing console was not completed yet. Without this activation, tags exist as metadata on resources but are invisible to Cost Explorer's reporting layer. Additionally, even after activation, Cost Explorer only shows tag data for costs incurred AFTER the activation date — historical costs before activation cannot be retroactively attributed by tag.
tasks.fix: Go to the AWS Billing console → Cost Allocation Tags → activate Team, Environment, and Owner. Cost Explorer will begin showing these as filterable dimensions for new costs immediately; historical pre-activation costs will remain unattributable by tag. For Meera's board meeting tomorrow: be honest that the tag data will be available from today's costs forward, but historical breakdown requires estimation from service-level data combined with known ownership.
tasks.explanation: This two-step process's real gotcha — tag in resource irundhaalum, in billing activate without doing, Cost in Explorer kaanaaathu. AND historical costs retroactively appear aagathu — only going-forward. for Meera honest answer: from today forward, not retroactively.

FoodQuick Production Architecture — Current State (post CS2-CS6):

COMPUTE (CS4/FQ-171):

what_to_find: The architecture is coherent and deliberate — every component was reasoned through, not accumulated accidentally
Security is defense-in-depth: IAM least-privilege at account level, SG restrictions at resource level, BPA at bucket level, encryption in transit and at rest
Reliability is Multi-AZ at every stateful layer (RDS, ASG, NAT Gateways) with verified failover behavior

The architecture has known, documented remaining gaps (IaC coverage not complete for S3/CloudWatch/IAM, load testing framework not yet in place) — gaps a student can name specifically are better than unexamined unknowns
tasks.correct_fix: No changes needed — this is the architecture review task. The job here is to be able to explain every component, its reason for being where it is, and what trade-off it represents. A student who can walk through this diagram and explain each decision is ready for CS7's final lesson.
tasks.explanation: This capstone 'recognize this is already correct' task — but this also the student's architecture to explain, not just audit. Ovva component also in CS2-CS6 we saw lessons's result. This Building Basics's whole point.

tasks.scenario: Meera's board meeting is tomorrow. With tag activation done today, historical cost attribution by tag isn't possible yet — but she needs something for the board. You use service-level Cost Explorer data plus known ownership to construct an estimated per-team breakdown for the past quarter. Total AWS spend last quarter: ₹11.2L.
tasks.question: How should this estimated breakdown be framed honestly for a board audience — given it's estimated from service data, not from clean tag attribution?
tasks.solution: Estimated breakdown (from service-level data + ownership mapping): Order Engineering: ~₹4.8L (EC2 order-service, ALB, RDS orders-db primary) | Platform Engineering: ~₹2.9L (networking, NAT Gateways, bastion, Reserved Instances admin overhead) | Analytics: ~₹1.7L (reporting-db-01, S3 exports, Logs Insights queries) | DevOps/Monitoring: ~₹0.4L (CloudWatch, CloudTrail, X-Ray) | Unattributed/Shared: ~₹1.4L (S3 cross-team buckets, partial overlap). Frame honestly: 'These are estimates based on service ownership mapping, not clean tag data. From today's billing cycle forward, we will have exact per-team attribution through cost allocation tags. The estimates are directionally correct but should not be treated as precise.'
tasks.explanation: This real business communication — honest about what's estimated vs exact, useful numbers kudukkadhu, 'we can't tell you anything' — refusal not. 'Directionally correct, not precise' — right level of confidence for estimated data.
